newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bavarian CSU says EMU must wait for strength.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bavarian CSU says EMU must wait for strength.

text.p: Bavaria's Christian Social Union (CSU), a core part of the ruling Bonn coalition, made it clear on Wednesday it would prefer to see Europe's single currency delayed rather than risk it being weak.

Edmund Stoiber, the powerful CSU premier of Germany's large southern state, said Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) must wait until would-be participants adhered strictly to the entry criteria laid out in the Maastricht Treaty.
"Economic and monetary union either begins on January 1, 1999 as a union of stability, or it must be delayed until the preconditions are met," Stoiber said in a speech in Munich.

Stoiber's view was backed up by separate comments by German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, party leader of the CSU, who later repeated his line that EMU criteria should determine the timetable for the project, which is due to start in 1999.
It was "absolutely necessary" that the economic convergence criteria laid out by the Maastricht Treaty be adhered to strictly, said Waigel, who was speaking at an industry symposium in Bonn.

Stoiber, who was outlining the position of the Bavarian state government on European issues ahead of next week's EU summit in Amsterdam, also warned France against upsetting the "consensus of stability" on which the project was built.

He pointed in particular to concerns that the newly-elected French government might not ratify the so-called stability pact, a German initiative aimed at securing the stability of the future euro currency.
"I can only hope that the stability pact remains unadulterated," he said.

Paris earlier this week said it might not be ready by the time of the summit to agree the pact, which would allow for EMU participants to be fined if their economies did not live up to agreed measures of performance. It has since indicated it might after all ratify the deal.
The CSU, the sister party of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), has established itself as Europe's most vocal political force behind a "hard" economic and monetary union.
Domestically, comments such as Stoiber's seek to position the CSU as the staunchest defender of the deutschemark against a euro that might not match the strength of the German currency.

Last week there were reports the members of the CSU might actively push for a delay of EMU following the election of the Socialist-led government in France, whom they fear would seek to loosen the criteria for entry into the currency union.
A further concern for the right-of-centre CSU is that Paris might now lead a march to introduce an expensive employment chapter into the EU treaty in Amsterdam.

"Jobs programmes only work when they are backed by lots of money and it would be mainly Germany that would be called on to finance these programmes," Bavarian CSU state minister Kurt Faltlhauser said in speech preceeding Stoiber's in Munich.

Faltlhauser said it would be unacceptable if an employment chapter in the EU treaty was agreed which allowed job creation programmes to be launched with the backing of only a qualified majority of member states.
"I can only hope that Chancellor Helmut Kohl succeeds in Amsterdam in pulling the rudder back round again when it comes to the formulation of the employment chapter," Faltlhauser said.
